sections.section_title: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease

blocks.text: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is an immune-mediated inflammatory complication of group A streptococcal infection. Recurrent episodes can cause progressive rheumatic heart disease (RHD), particularly mitral and aortic valve damage. Treatment has four central components: eradication of residual streptococci, control of inflammation and symptoms, management of cardiac complications, and long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis.
The 2024 WHO guideline provides current recommendations for prevention, diagnosis and secondary prophylaxis, while the CDC's 2025 clinical guidance outlines acute treatment principles.

Critical safety principle: Acute rheumatic fever with significant carditis, heart failure, severe valve dysfunction, arrhythmia or neurological complications requires hospital assessment and specialist-led treatment. Secondary prophylaxis is essential because recurrent attacks can cause further valve damage.

rows: Acute rheumatic fever without significant carditis
Streptococcal eradication, anti-inflammatory symptom control and secondary prophylaxis
As above, plus cardiac monitoring and assessment for valve dysfunction
Urgent heart failure management and specialist assessment of valve severity
Safety measures and symptom control; consider medication for severe or disabling symptoms
Secondary prophylaxis, surveillance and management of valve disease
RHD with atrial fibrillation or embolic risk
Severe mitral or aortic valve disease
Specialist evaluation for intervention, including balloon valvotomy or surgery where appropriate

items.text: Eradicate residual group A streptococci, even if throat symptoms have resolved.
Relieve arthritis, fever and other inflammatory symptoms.
Manage carditis, heart failure and arrhythmias.
Prevent recurrent rheumatic fever through reliable long-term antibiotic prophylaxis.
Detect and manage progressive valve disease before irreversible complications develop.

blocks.text: Antibiotic treatment is recommended for diagnosed acute rheumatic fever even if current throat symptoms are absent or testing no longer demonstrates streptococci. This eradication regimen is separate from the long-term secondary prophylaxis regimen.

blocks.title: A common single-dose IM eradication regimen is:

items.text: Weight 27 kg or less: 600,000 units IM once.
Weight above 27 kg: 1.2 million units IM once.

blocks.text: Confirm the formulation and local protocol before administration.
**Example prescription — adult or child above 27 kg**
Rx
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units
Administer 1.2 million units by deep intramuscular injection once, if appropriate and there is no contraindication.
Quantity: one dose.
Important: This is a depot IM suspension, not an IV medicine. Verify the product name and formulation; do not administer intravenously or intrathecally.
Where IM treatment is unsuitable, an oral course can be used according to the local group A streptococcal eradication guideline. A common adult regimen is:

items.text: Penicillin V 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days.

blocks.text: Paediatric dosing must be weight- and age-appropriate and remain within the recommended maximum dose.
Do not prescribe penicillin automatically in a patient with a history of immediate anaphylaxis, angioedema or a severe delayed reaction such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Alternative antibiotic selection depends on the type of reaction, local resistance and the current guideline. A macrolide may be an option in selected patients, but resistance must be considered. For severe allergy histories, obtain specialist or antimicrobial stewardship advice.
Prescribing pearl: Eradication treatment does not replace long-term secondary prophylaxis in a patient with confirmed ARF or RHD.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Anti-inflammatory treatment for acute rheumatic fever

blocks.text: Anti-inflammatory medicines are used mainly to relieve arthritis, fever and inflammation. They have not been established as reliably preventing chronic valve damage. The 2024 WHO guideline did not make a recommendation for or against anti-inflammatory agents specifically to prevent progression to RHD.
Naproxen is a commonly used option for significant rheumatic arthritis when an NSAID is appropriate.
**Example adult prescription**
Rx
Naproxen 250–500 mg orally every 12 hours with food.

Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest clinically appropriate period, then reassess symptoms and adverse effects. The exact dose and duration should follow the patient's age, weight, renal function and local protocol.
**Contraindications and precautions**

items.text: Active peptic ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Significant renal impairment, dehydration or decompensated heart failure.
NSAID hypersensitivity or aspirin-sensitive asthma.
Concomitant anticoagulants or other NSAIDs, which increase bleeding risk.
Pregnancy, particularly from 20 weeks onward and especially in the third trimester, unless specifically directed by a clinician.

blocks.text: Aspirin has historically been used for acute rheumatic arthritis. Because it can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, salicylism and toxicity, high-dose regimens should be clinician-supervised, particularly in children.

A paediatric anti-inflammatory regimen used in some protocols is approximately 50–60 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses, adjusted to response and local guidance. Do not exceed the protocol's maximum dose. Monitor for tinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation, altered mental status, gastrointestinal bleeding and hepatic toxicity.

Important: Avoid aspirin in children and adolescents with a suspected viral illness because of the association with Reye syndrome. For rheumatic fever, choose the anti-inflammatory regimen according to the treating team's protocol rather than combining aspirin with another NSAID.
Corticosteroids may be considered by specialists in selected patients with severe carditis or particular complications, but evidence that they prevent chronic RHD is limited.
They are not routine treatment for every case of ARF.

If used, document the indication, dose, tapering plan and monitoring for hyperglycaemia, hypertension, infection, gastrointestinal effects and other steroid-related complications. Significant valve disease or heart failure requires appropriate cardiac management regardless of whether corticosteroids are given.

Mild chorea may improve with supportive care and protection from injury. Severe or disabling chorea may require specialist-directed medication, such as valproate or carbamazepine, depending on the patient and contraindications. Corticosteroids or other immunomodulatory therapy may be considered in selected severe cases.

items.text: Valproate: avoid in pregnancy when possible and observe strict reproductive safety precautions in patients who could become pregnant.
Carbamazepine: check sodium, blood count, liver function and drug interactions; serious skin reactions are possible.
Consider school, mobility, nutrition and psychological support where relevant.

blocks.text: Do not use a single universal drug regimen for chorea without considering age, severity, pregnancy potential and comorbidities.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis: the cornerstone of prevention

blocks.text: Secondary prophylaxis reduces recurrent group A streptococcal infection and further rheumatic fever attacks. WHO recommends antibiotic prophylaxis for patients diagnosed with ARF or RHD and identifies intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin as the preferred first-line option. Oral penicillin is an alternative when IM treatment is not feasible.

items.text: Body weight 27 kg or less: 600,000 units IM every 4 weeks.
Body weight above 27 kg: 1.2 million units IM every 4 weeks.

blocks.text: In selected patients with recurrent attacks despite adherence, or in high-risk settings, a specialist may prescribe a shorter interval, commonly every 3 weeks, according to the relevant guideline.
Rx
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units
Administer 1.2 million units by deep IM injection every 4 weeks for secondary prevention, if the patient weighs above 27 kg and has no contraindication.
Quantity: One dose per scheduled administration; prescribe sufficient supply according to the planned follow-up period and local dispensing rules.
Review: Document the next injection date, intended duration of prophylaxis, allergy status and a system for tracking missed doses.
**Administration safety**

items.text: Confirm that the product is benzathine benzylpenicillin for IM use—not aqueous benzylpenicillin or another penicillin formulation.
Give by the recommended deep IM technique and follow the product's reconstitution instructions.
Never administer benzathine benzylpenicillin intravenously or intrathecally.
Observe local procedures for allergy risk, injection safety and management of anaphylaxis.
Discuss injection pain and strategies to improve adherence.

blocks.text: **B. Oral penicillin V for secondary prophylaxis**
When regular IM injections are not possible, an oral alternative may be used.

items.text: Penicillin V 250 mg orally twice daily, continuously for the prescribed prophylaxis period.

blocks.text: Paediatric doses and maximum doses must follow the applicable guideline. Oral prophylaxis is more dependent on daily adherence than depot IM treatment.
**C. Penicillin allergy**

For a patient with a confirmed penicillin allergy, alternatives can include a macrolide or sulfadiazine, depending on the reaction history, age, pregnancy status, local resistance and current guideline.

items.text: Do not prescribe a cephalosporin automatically for someone with a history of penicillin anaphylaxis or severe delayed hypersensitivity.
Check QT-prolongation risks and interactions before selecting a macrolide.
Sulfadiazine is not appropriate for every patient; assess allergy, renal function, blood disorders and pregnancy-related precautions.
Consider specialist review to clarify the allergy when the history is uncertain and safe testing is available.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. How long should secondary prophylaxis continue?

blocks.text: The duration depends on the history of ARF, presence and severity of carditis, residual valve disease, recurrence risk, age and local guidelines. There is no single end date appropriate for everyone.

rows: At least 5 years after the last attack or until age 21 years, whichever is longer
ARF with carditis but no residual valve disease
At least 10 years after the last attack or until age 21 years, whichever is longer
At least 10 years after the last attack or until age 40 years, whichever is longer
Severe RHD, previous valve surgery or ongoing high exposure risk
May require longer-term or lifelong prophylaxis; specialist review is essential

blocks.text: These are commonly used guideline frameworks; national recommendations differ, and some patients should continue longer. Decisions to stop prophylaxis should be made with the treating team after reassessing valve status, recurrence risk and exposure risk.
High-yield point: Missing injections is a preventable risk factor for recurrent ARF. Use appointment reminders, an injection register, community follow-up and clear patient education.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. Management of rheumatic heart disease and valve complications

blocks.text: Established RHD requires treatment of the haemodynamic consequences of valve damage, not just antibiotics. Secondary prophylaxis does not reverse established stenosis or regurgitation.

blocks.title: For clinically significant rheumatic mitral stenosis:

items.text: Use a diuretic when pulmonary or systemic congestion is present.
Control ventricular rate if atrial fibrillation or another tachyarrhythmia is contributing to symptoms.
Assess anticoagulation if atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus or previous systemic embolism is present.
Refer for assessment of percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy or surgery when indicated.

blocks.text: Percutaneous balloon commissurotomy is appropriate only for selected patients with suitable valve anatomy and without important contraindications, such as left atrial thrombus or more than mild mitral regurgitation.
Management depends on the severity of regurgitation, ventricular response and symptoms.

items.text: Diuretics may relieve congestion but do not correct the valve lesion.
Treat hypertension and heart failure according to the relevant clinical indication.
Arrange serial echocardiography and specialist review.
Refer for valve intervention when symptoms, ventricular dysfunction, ventricular dimensions or other guideline criteria indicate it.

content_groups.group_title: C. Heart failure due to RHD

blocks.text: If congestion is present, a loop diuretic such as furosemide may be required.

A common adult starting regimen is furosemide 20–40 mg orally once daily, adjusted to clinical response, renal function, electrolytes and severity. In acute decompensation, IV treatment and monitored care may be required.

items.text: Blood pressure, fluid balance and daily weight where appropriate.
Renal function, sodium, potassium and magnesium.
Symptoms of hypotension, dehydration and electrolyte depletion.

blocks.text: Do not automatically apply all four standard heart failure drug classes to every patient with RHD. Treatment depends on whether there is reduced ejection fraction, preserved ejection fraction, significant valve obstruction or regurgitation, and whether the patient is compensated or acutely decompensated.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Atrial fibrillation and anticoagulation in RHD

blocks.text: Atrial fibrillation is particularly important in rheumatic mitral stenosis because it can increase the risk of left atrial thrombus and systemic embolism.

items.text: Moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF: warfarin is generally preferred over a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC).
A usual warfarin target is INR 2.0–3.0, unless a different target is required by the specific indication, such as a mechanical valve.
Mechanical prosthetic valves require valve-specific anticoagulation targets and specialist monitoring.
Do not use a DOAC as a routine substitute for warfarin in moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF.

blocks.text: Warfarin prescribing must include INR monitoring, interaction review and a plan for missed doses, procedures and bleeding. A patient with RHD who is in sinus rhythm does not automatically need anticoagulation; the indication must be assessed individually.

rows: Assess valve stenosis/regurgitation, ventricular function, chamber size and pulmonary pressures
Detect atrial fibrillation and other rhythm or conduction abnormalities
Monitor diuretics and other heart failure medicines
Assess recurrent ARF, heart failure, embolic events and treatment tolerance

blocks.text: Follow-up intervals depend on valve severity, symptoms, age and the risk of recurrence. Patients with severe valve disease, worsening symptoms, new atrial fibrillation or heart failure need expedited specialist review.
Pregnancy increases circulatory demands and can destabilise significant mitral stenosis or other severe valve disease.

items.text: Patients with moderate-to-severe RHD should receive preconception counselling and specialist cardio-obstetric assessment where possible.
Diuretics may be needed for congestion but must be carefully titrated.
Warfarin and other anticoagulants require an individualised pregnancy plan, particularly for mechanical valves; do not switch or stop anticoagulation without specialist advice.
Secondary prophylaxis should be maintained using a pregnancy-appropriate plan.
Avoid selecting medicines solely on their usual non-pregnant regimen; verify pregnancy-specific safety and monitoring.

rows: Verify allergy history and formulation; IM only
Confirm adherence and assess severe allergy
Gastrointestinal bleeding, renal injury; aspirin toxicity
Avoid duplicate NSAIDs; assess bleeding and renal risks
Monitor electrolytes, renal function and fluid status
INR monitoring, interaction review and pregnancy planning
Specialist oversight and strict reproductive safety precautions
Check blood count, sodium, liver function and interactions

items.text: Giving the one-time streptococcal eradication dose but failing to prescribe secondary prophylaxis.
Confusing benzathine benzylpenicillin with other penicillin formulations.
Administering a depot benzathine penicillin product intravenously.
Prescribing the same prophylaxis interval and duration for every patient regardless of valve disease and recurrence risk.
Treating arthritis with high-dose NSAIDs without checking renal function, gastrointestinal risk and other medicines.
Using a DOAC routinely in moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation.
Assuming antibiotics alone will treat severe valve dysfunction or heart failure.
Failing to create a system to follow up missed injections.
Treat group A streptococcal infection appropriately to prevent initial ARF.
Patients with ARF or RHD generally need long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis.
IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is the preferred first-line option when feasible.
Anti-inflammatory drugs help control symptoms but have not been proven to prevent chronic RHD.
Carditis with heart failure or severe valve dysfunction requires urgent cardiac assessment.
Warfarin is generally preferred for AF with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.
Established valve disease requires echocardiographic surveillance and intervention when indicated.
A robust system for prophylaxis adherence is part of treatment, not an optional extra.
